scams.name: Taxi Bill-Switch and Counterfeit Change
scams.description:
Santa Marta's unmetered taxis run on agreed fares, which means every payment involves cash handed across the seat. Tourists arrive with large bills — 20,000- and 50,000-peso notes dispensed in bulk by ATMs — while most fares sit between 10,000 and 15,000 pesos, so change must be made. That brief moment of the driver handling your note is the entire setup.

The driver accepts your 20,000-peso note, turns briefly away, then holds up a 2,000-peso note: "You only gave me 2,000." He has palmed the larger bill in a rehearsed move. The counterfeit variant runs in reverse — the driver takes your 50,000-peso note, returns it claiming it is fake or he has no change, and the next day a shopkeeper tells you the bill you are holding is counterfeit. The driver kept your real note.

Carry 5,000- and 10,000-peso notes and pay the exact fare whenever possible. State the denomination aloud as you hand it over — "Here is twenty thousand pesos" — so the driver cannot credibly claim you passed a smaller bill. For larger fares, use InDriver, Didi, or Uber, where the fare is locked digitally before you enter the vehicle and the bill-exchange moment never occurs.
scams.avoidance: Carry small bills (5,000 and 10,000 peso notes) and pay with exact change whenever possible State the denomination out loud as you hand it to the driver: 'Here is twenty thousand pesos' Agree on the fare before entering the taxi and have the exact amount ready Use ride-hailing apps like InDriver, Didi, or Uber where payment is handled digitally Familiarize yourself with Colombian bill denominations and security features before arriving — check returned bills for watermarks
scams.location: Taxis throughout Santa Marta, especially outside hotels in El Rodadero, the Centro Histórico, and near Parque de los Novios at night
scams.tldr: Taxi drivers across Santa Marta palm tourists' large-denomination peso notes during fare payment or swap them for counterfeit bills, costing riders 10,000–50,000 pesos per trip on routes between El Rodadero, the Centro Histórico, and hotels throughout the city.

scams.name: Fake Police Document Inspection
scams.description:
The approach happens in daylight on the busy tourist streets of Santa Marta's Centro Histórico. The uniforms are close enough to the Colombian National Police uniform to pass a quick glance: dark shirts, badge-shaped patches, lanyards with official-looking ID cards. They select solo tourists or small groups who appear distracted, with documents and wallets visible.

One officer requests your documents; the other asks to inspect your wallet for counterfeit bills. While the first examines your passport, the second rifles through your wallet, counting and pocketing bills under the guise of checking serial numbers. They issue a handwritten "receipt" and direct you to the nearest police station to recover the money. Real officers at the station confirm no such inspection occurred — the receipt is worthless.

Real Colombian police do not inspect tourist wallets on the street for counterfeit currency. If anyone in a uniform asks to inspect your wallet, say you will walk with them to the nearest Policía Nacional office to verify their credentials — genuine officers will agree, and scammers will not. Keep only a photocopy of your passport photo page in your pocket and leave the original in your hotel safe so you have nothing critical to hand over.
scams.avoidance: Leave your passport at the hotel safe and carry only a photocopy of the photo page and entry stamps If approached by supposed police, politely request to see their official photo ID and badge number Suggest walking to the nearest police station to verify their identity — real officers will agree, scammers will not Never hand over your wallet — if asked for ID, hold it yourself and let them look at it in your hands Call 123 (Colombian police emergency) to verify any officer's identity before complying with demands
scams.location: Streets around the Centro Histórico, Parque de los Novios, walkways near Taganga, and roads near popular tourist sites
scams.tldr: Two men in convincing near-police uniforms stop tourists near Parque de los Novios for a "counterfeit bill check," pocket cash during the wallet inspection, and issue a worthless handwritten receipt — a coordinated street robbery that empties wallets in under five minutes.

scams.name: Beach Distraction Theft
scams.description:
Santa Marta's beaches are social and relaxed, which is exactly what makes them productive for theft teams. Bags pile up on towels while tourists swim — phone, cash for the day, sometimes a camera. Vendors and strangers circulate continuously along the shoreline, and the easy atmosphere at El Rodadero and Taganga makes someone approaching your belongings unremarkable.

One team member moves toward your unattended bag from the shore side while an accomplice creates the distraction: a beach ball thrown near your things, a loud exchange among nearby beachgoers, or a vendor engaging you in the water. In the moment your attention shifts, the first person lifts your phone and wallet from the bag and walks away at a normal pace. An alternate version targets you directly in the water — someone offers drinks or sunglasses while their partner works the bags on shore.

The only reliable defense is giving theft teams nothing to take. Leave your phone, passport, and excess cash at the hotel and bring only what you can wear or carry into the water with you. A waterproof pouch worn around your neck removes the vulnerability entirely. If you travel with a companion, take turns swimming so someone always has eyes on the bags; solo travelers at Tayrona or Taganga should treat the sand as a no-storage zone.
scams.avoidance: Never leave valuables unattended on the beach — bring only what you need for the day and leave everything else at the hotel Use a waterproof phone pouch that you can take into the water with you Take turns swimming with a travel companion so someone always watches the belongings Use a portable beach safe or lockbox that you can secure to a fixed object like a beach chair At Tayrona Park or Taganga, bring only essentials: cash for food, a cheap phone, and sunscreen
scams.location: Playa El Rodadero, Taganga Beach, Playa Blanca, and beach areas around Parque Nacional Natural Tayrona
scams.tldr: Coordinated teams at Playa El Rodadero, Taganga, and Tayrona steal phones, wallets, and cameras from unattended beach bags while accomplices distract tourists in or near the water — a loss that can include every valuable left on the sand.

scams.name: Scopolamine (Devil's Breath) Drink Spiking
scams.description:
The approach is social and unhurried. A woman starts a conversation at a bar in El Rodadero or the Centro Histórico, or a match on a dating app suggests meeting at a specific venue. She is attentive and friendly, and offers to buy the first round. The setting is a normal bar, the drink arrives sealed or from the bartender, and nothing seems wrong.

Scopolamine — known locally as burundanga — is colorless, odorless, and tasteless. A fraction of a gram is enough. Within minutes the victim feels dizzy and agreeable, is escorted back to the hotel, and willingly opens the door, hands over the phone passcode, opens the safe. The drug eliminates the brain's ability to form memories during the episode. The victim wakes hours later with no memory of any of it, and the wallet, phone, watch, and laptop are gone.

The risk compounds sharply when strangers suggest moving to your hotel room. Never accept a drink from someone you just met, and if you set your drink down for any reason, order a new one rather than returning to it. Go out with trusted companions and agree on a check-in protocol — if anyone in the group seems suddenly disoriented or unusually agreeable after one or two drinks, get them out of the bar and to a safe location immediately. Documented incidents consistently involve drinks accepted from new acquaintances in El Rodadero's bar district.
scams.avoidance: Never accept drinks from strangers and never leave your drink unattended — get a new one if you stepped away Avoid bringing strangers to your hotel room, especially people met at bars or through dating apps Go out with trusted friends and watch out for each other — if someone seems suddenly out of it, get them to safety immediately Use drink covers or bottle toppers to prevent anything being dropped into your beverage If you feel suddenly disoriented after a drink, tell a trusted person immediately and get to a safe location
scams.location: Bars and nightclubs in El Rodadero, late-night establishments in the Centro Histórico, and encounters initiated through dating apps
scams.tldr: Strangers at El Rodadero bars — often attractive women — spike tourists' drinks with scopolamine (burundanga), a colorless and odorless drug that causes compliance and memory loss while accomplices clear hotel rooms of phones, laptops, watches, and cash.

scams.name: Overpriced Unofficial Tour Guide
scams.description:
The gate at Tayrona National Park and the Santa Marta departure points for the Lost City trek draw a steady crowd of informal vendors, taxi drivers, and apparent guides. A confident, knowledgeable-seeming man approaches as tourists arrive, walking them through the layout of the park and offering a "private tour" at what sounds like a reasonable rate — 80,000 pesos for a full-day guide who knows the trails and beaches.

Once inside the park, the guide provides scattered commentary, spends long stretches on his phone, and moves through the trails too quickly for real interpretation. At the beaches, he declares the tour complete and disappears. The tourist discovers afterward that self-guided entry costs only 20,000 pesos, and certified guides with proper ecological and historical training charge 50,000–60,000 pesos through the park's official office. For the Lost City trek, only four licensed operators are authorized by the government; anyone else is operating illegally regardless of how professional they present.

The gate is where the pressure is highest and the time to verify is shortest. Book Tayrona and Lost City tours only through agencies with verified reviews on TripAdvisor or GetYourGuide, and ask to see the guide's official license before paying anything at the gate. For Ciudad Perdida, the authorized operators are Expotur, Wiwa Tour, Turcol, and Magic Tour — any other offer is unlicensed. Researching standard prices before you arrive makes it easy to spot both overcharging and suspiciously cheap last-minute offers at the entrance.
scams.avoidance: Book tours through licensed agencies with verified reviews on TripAdvisor, Google, or GetYourGuide For the Lost City trek, only book with one of the few licensed operators (Expotur, Wiwa Tour, Turcol, or Magic Tour) Ask for official guide credentials and verify them with the tourism office if in doubt Get a written agreement including the itinerary, inclusions, and refund policy before paying Research the standard price for any tour before arriving so you can spot both overcharging and suspiciously low offers
scams.location: Outside the entrance to Parque Nacional Natural Tayrona, Minca coffee farm tours, Lost City (Ciudad Perdida) trek departures, and around Santa Marta's harbor
scams.tldr: Unlicensed men at the gates of Tayrona National Park and Ciudad Perdida trek departure points sell "private guided tours" for 80,000+ pesos while delivering little — a straightforward overcharge when legitimate park entry costs 20,000 pesos and certified guides charge 50,000–60,000 pesos through official channels.

scams.name: Bird Poop and Bracelet Distraction Theft
scams.description:
The Centro Histórico around the cathedral and Parque de los Novios is the primary zone for both techniques. Tourists pass through with bags at their sides, distracted by the architecture and activity. A team of two to four people selects a target and tracks them to a moment that is busy enough to provide cover but not so crowded that the approach draws attention.

Someone taps your shoulder and points to a white substance on your jacket — "bird poop!" A second person materializes immediately with napkins, leaning in close to help clean the stain and apologizing. While you look down at the mess, a third team member behind you slips a hand into your pocket or unzips your bag. The bracelet variant is gentler: a person ties a colorful bracelet on your wrist as a "free gift," then demands payment. While you argue about the price, accomplices position themselves near your valuables.

Stopping in place is what the operation depends on — the pickpocket behind you works in the seconds while you inspect the stain. If anyone points out a mark on your clothing, do not stop: walk immediately to a nearby shop or café before looking down at it. For bracelets, the moment to refuse is before contact — step back and say no firmly before anything is tied to your wrist, because social pressure to pay starts the instant the bracelet is on. In the Centro Histórico, carry your bag in front and keep your phone in a zipped inner pocket.
scams.avoidance: If someone points out a stain, do not stop — walk away to a safe area before inspecting your clothing Do not accept 'free' bracelets, flowers, or gifts from strangers — decline firmly and keep walking Wear your bag on your front in the Centro Histórico and keep your phone in a zipped inner pocket Travel with a companion when possible so someone can watch your back during unexpected interactions Be especially alert near the cathedral and Parque de los Novios where these teams operate most actively
scams.location: Centro Histórico around the cathedral, Parque de los Novios, beachfront promenades, and busy pedestrian streets near Rodadero
scams.tldr: Teams of two to four in Santa Marta's Centro Histórico spray a white substance on tourists' clothing and "helpfully" clean it while pickpocketing them, or tie bracelets on wrists as "free gifts" and demand 50,000–100,000 pesos — a coordinated street operation targeting anyone walking with bags in tourist areas.

scams.name: Attempted Knifepoint Robbery Near Historic Center
scams.description:
Santa Marta's well-lit tourist corridors are patrolled and relatively safe after dark: the Parque de los Novios area, the main promenade at El Rodadero, the busiest restaurant streets. The risk concentrates on the transitions — the side alleys connecting restaurants to hotels, the blocks between the tourist district and less-developed neighborhoods, and the poorly lit approach roads into Taganga.

Two young men emerge from a doorway or the shadow of a parked car, one holding a knife. The demand is immediate: phone, wallet, watch, now. The robbery is over in under a minute. Hesitation or any negotiation escalates the confrontation; victims who have attempted to resist or run describe the interaction turning physical. The attackers move fast and have done this before.

The vulnerability is the gap between a bar door and a hotel lobby on streets where you are alone and the lighting is poor. Use Uber, InDriver, or a hotel-arranged taxi for any movement after dark between nightlife and your accommodation — even for distances that seem walkable. Ask your hotel which specific streets are safe to walk at night; staff know the current situation block by block and will tell you exactly where the risk concentrates. Leave expensive watches, jewelry, and visible electronics at the hotel safe before going out in the evening.
scams.avoidance: Never walk on side streets in Santa Marta after dark — use Uber, InDriver, or a hotel-arranged taxi even for short distances Stick to well-lit, well-trafficked streets like Carrera 1 and the Parque de los Novios area when out at night Do not wear expensive jewelry, watches, or visible electronics when walking around the city If confronted, hand over your belongings without resistance — nothing is worth your safety Ask your hotel which specific streets are safe to walk at night and which to avoid
scams.location: Side streets off the Centro Histórico at night, dark streets near Taganga, and poorly lit areas between bars and hotels
scams.tldr: Two-person robbery teams on side streets off Santa Marta's Centro Histórico and near Taganga brandish knives and demand phones, wallets, and watches from tourists walking between bars and hotels after dark — a 30-second crime on streets that look walkable but are not safe at night.
